notes.h: Dual-earner families and changing sex roles
notes.b: Reconciling paid work with family life depends on how a household divides its roles and tasks between its members. Over time, the roles people expect of men and women have changed, and that change shapes how dual-earner families run.
points: A dual-earner family (also called a dual-career family) is one in which both partners are in paid employment, so the household has two incomes and two sets of work demands.

A role is the set of behaviours and responsibilities expected of a person in a position such as parent, employee, partner or homemaker (the person who runs the home). Sex roles, also called gender roles, are the tasks and behaviour expected of men and women.
Traditional sex roles gave the man the main earning role, as breadwinner, and the woman the main responsibility for childcare and home care, as homemaker.
Sex roles have loosened as more women take up paid work and more men take an active part in childcare and housework, so tasks are increasingly shared rather than fixed by sex.
Fathers can now take paternity leave and parent's leave, and some families have a stay-at-home father, which shows that caring is no longer seen as only a woman's job.
The change is real but not complete: attitudes have changed, yet women on average still do more of the household and caring work.
Children learn sex roles from the way tasks are shared at home, as well as from school, peers and the media, so what they see their parents do shapes what they expect for themselves.
notes.tip: Do not claim that all families now share equally. Say the pattern is changing and that women still often carry more. Define role, sex role and dual-earner family, because exams ask for these definitions.

notes.b: When both partners work, someone still has to do the childcare and the housework. Role overload is what happens when one person is asked to do too many of these jobs at once.
points: Role overload occurs when one person tries to perform several roles at the same time, for example employee, parent, homemaker and carer, and cannot meet the demands of all of them. It is about too many roles to cope with at once.
Effects on the individual: less leisure and rest time, tiredness, stress and poorer health, with a risk of burnout (complete exhaustion from long-term stress) if the load continues.

Effects on work: difficulty finding time for training, extra hours or promotion, and less energy for them, because the person has little left after the demands of home. There may also be pressure to take work home.
Effects on the family: tension between partners and other family members, less time with children, and neglect of family and household tasks that no one has time to do.
Vulnerable members, such as young children, an elderly relative or a family member who is ill, may have no one available to care for them.
Women often carry a larger share of the strain because they usually remain the main carers at home, so they end up doing a full job and then the home tasks as well.

Overload can be reduced by sharing tasks, using labour-saving appliances, buying in outside help such as a cleaner or childcare, keeping routines simple, planning meals, and using leave and flexible work arrangements.
notes.tip: Role overload is not role conflict. Define overload as too many roles to cope with at once, and give it its own example, such as an employee who is also a parent and homemaker and cannot meet all the demands.

notes.b: Role conflict is a different problem from overload. Here a person may be able to manage each role, but two roles pull in opposite directions at the same moment and a choice has to be made.
points: Role conflict arises when the expectations of one role clash with the expectations of another, so that both cannot be met and one has to give way. It is two roles pulling in different directions.
Example: a child becomes sick and needs a parent at home while a work deadline or meeting requires the same parent to be at work.
Priority choice: a parent must decide which role to put first at a given moment, and that decision often causes guilt about the role that lost out.
Conflict between partners: one partner may not support the other's employment, or the couple may compete over career priorities, so each feels the other is getting in the way.
Conflict with the employer: an employer may expect availability, such as late meetings or travel, that clashes with school hours and childcare arrangements.
Effects include stress, guilt, and tension and arguments between partners. Employment may suffer through absence or missed promotion.
Outcome for the family: children may feel lonely or neglected, and the family may need outside help to resolve the conflict.
notes.tip: Keep conflict apart from overload and give it its own example, such as the sick child and the work deadline. In a question on dual-earner families, define each term, give an effect on family members, and say how parents share duties.

notes.h: Distribution of parental and home-care responsibilities
notes.b: Every household has two sets of jobs: caring for the children and caring for the home. How a dual-earner couple divides them decides whether the family copes or falls into overload and conflict.
points: Parental responsibilities include feeding, dressing, supervising, school runs and collections, helping with homework, health care, emotional support, discipline and play, and transporting and supporting children.
Home-care responsibilities include cooking, cleaning, laundry, shopping, budgeting, bills, repairs, the garden and maintaining the home.
Fair sharing: in the modern pattern, partners agree which tasks each one owns, so that tasks are not done only when one partner asks for help. Fathers are more involved in childcare.
Labour-saving appliances, such as washing machines, dishwashers, microwave ovens and slow cookers, reduce the time needed for home-care tasks, which frees time for the family.
Outside help, such as paid childcare, a childminder, cleaning services, or grandparents and other relatives, takes over some parental and home-care duties.
Older children can take on age-appropriate tasks, such as tidying their rooms or setting the table, which builds independence.

Benefits of sharing: less overload, stronger parent-child bonds including father-child bonds, and fairer family relationships. When both parents take an active part in care, children see shared parenting as normal, which models gender equality and shows that men and women have equal roles.

Drawbacks if tasks are not shared or are poorly managed: resentment and arguments, one partner carrying a double shift (a full day of paid work followed by the home tasks), and children given too much responsibility.
notes.tip: When asked how parents share duties, name specific parental and home-care tasks and the ways of sharing them: agreement, appliances, outside help, relatives and age-appropriate jobs for children.

notes.h: Impact of dual-earner families on family life
notes.b: Having two earners changes family life in both good and bad ways. The balance depends on how tasks are shared, how childcare is arranged and how flexible the employers are.
points: Positive: a second income raises household living standards and reduces financial worry, and it gives security if one job is lost.
Positive: both partners gain independence and self-esteem, and parents gain wider social contact through work.
Positive: children may become more independent when they take on responsibilities, and they see their parents working, which gives them a role model for work and equal roles.
Positive: when parents share tasks, children learn that care and housework are shared responsibilities.
Negative: less time for shared family activities, conversation and leisure, and tiredness and stress, which can weaken family relationships. The couple may also have less time for each other.
Negative: children may feel lonely, neglected or left out, especially at times such as after school or when they are ill.
Negative: extra responsibility falls on older children, who may become carers for younger siblings. Less time for home tasks can also mean meals eaten out or convenience foods.
Negative: childcare costs can absorb a large part of the second income, and the family may face role overload and role conflict.
notes.tip: Evaluation questions want both sides and a judgement. Give positives and negatives, then say the impact depends on how well tasks are shared, on the childcare available and on how flexible the employers are.

notes.h: Ways to reconcile employment with family responsibilities
notes.b: Employers and employees use working arrangements that give more control over when and where work is done, and families add supports at home. Together they make it easier to hold a job and care for a family.
points: Flexitime: the employee chooses start and finish times within agreed limits, so that the working day can fit around school hours.
Job-sharing: two employees share one full-time post, dividing the hours and responsibilities between them.

Parental leave: unpaid leave taken to care for a child, which may be taken in blocks or spread over an agreed period. Under the Parental Leave Act 1998 (as amended) it is 26 weeks unpaid leave per child under 12.

Other leave arrangements are provided under the Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004, the Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016, the Parent's Leave and Benefit Act 2019 and the Carer's Leave Act 2001, and force majeure leave covers family emergencies.
Career break: a temporary period of unpaid leave that allows the employee to return to the same job later.
Teleworking: working from home reduces commuting time and lets a parent be available around the home.

Part-time and term-time work: reduced hours allow the employee to be at home during school hours or school holidays. Compressed working week: longer working days over fewer days free up time for family commitments.

At home and at work: help from childcare, after-school care and relatives, sharing housework, labour-saving appliances, planning such as meal planning, shopping lists and online shopping, and family meetings to share the load. Employers can help with flexible hours, crèche facilities and understanding about family emergencies.
notes.tip: Name each arrangement and say how it helps a parent, for example flexitime fitting work around school hours. Mention childcare here only as one way of reconciling work and home.

notes.h: Investigation: survey of male and female roles in home tasks
notes.b: A class survey shows how real households divide tasks and whether traditional sex roles still hold. This investigation uses a questionnaire about twenty home tasks.
points: Aim: to find out how male and female family members share twenty named home tasks in a sample of households.
Method step 1: list twenty home tasks, such as cooking, ironing, grocery shopping, car maintenance, paying bills, childminding, gardening, cleaning the bathroom and DIY.
Method step 2: design a questionnaire that asks who usually does each task: mainly male, mainly female, shared or someone else.
Method step 3: survey a sample of students, or their parents, and ask respondents to answer about their own household.
Method step 4: keep responses anonymous, so that no family or individual can be identified and people can answer honestly.
Analysis: count the answers in each category for each task and express each category as a percentage of the total answers, so you can find which tasks are mostly male, mostly female or shared.

Conclusion: the results show whether the sample's home tasks are still divided on traditional sex-role lines or are shared. Compare the results with traditional roles and link them to dual-earner households.
Limits: a small sample, bias in who answers and how honest the answers are can all weaken the conclusions.
notes.tip: A practical question asks for the aim, method and results. State the aim, list the tasks and the answer categories, say the answers are anonymous, and give results as counts and percentages.

keyTerms.definition: A family in which both partners are in paid employment.
The behaviours and responsibilities that a society or family expects of men and women.
The strain that results when one person tries to perform several roles at the same time and cannot meet all their demands.
The clash between the expectations of one role and the expectations of another role, such as work and parenthood.
The duties of caring for, supervising, supporting and guiding children.
The tasks of maintaining the home and feeding and clothing the family, such as cooking, cleaning and laundry.
A working arrangement in which employees choose their start and finish times within agreed limits.
An arrangement in which two people share one full-time job, splitting its hours and responsibilities.
Unpaid leave taken by a parent to care for a child.
A temporary period of unpaid leave from work that allows an employee to return to the same job later.
Doing paid work from home, using a computer and communication links rather than travelling to a workplace.

factCards.term: Three effects of role overload on family members
factCards.definition: 1. Reduced leisure and rest time. 2. Increased stress and tension between partners and family members. 3. Less time for each role, so work or family duties are neglected.

factCards.term: Four ways to share parental and home-care responsibilities
factCards.definition: 1. Agreeing a fair division of tasks between partners. 2. Using labour-saving appliances. 3. Getting outside help, such as paid childcare or relatives. 4. Giving older children age-appropriate jobs.

factCards.term: Four flexible working arrangements that help families
Two sources of conflict between partners in a dual-earner household
factCards.definition: 1. Disagreement over whose career takes priority. 2. One partner not supporting the other's paid work outside the home.

factCards.term: Three positive effects of dual-earner families on children
factCards.definition: 1. Children may become more independent. 2. Children learn that care and housework are shared. 3. Children see both parents actively involved in their upbringing.

factCards.term: First steps in the household task survey
factCards.definition: Choose twenty named home tasks, design a questionnaire asking who usually does each one, survey a sample anonymously, and count the answers in each category.

questions.prompt: Define role overload and state two effects it can have on a dual-earner family.
questions.model: Role overload: one person tries to perform several roles at the same time and cannot meet the demands of all of them. Effect 1: reduced leisure and rest time, leading to tiredness and stress. Effect 2: tension between partners and family members, or neglect of family tasks that no one has time to complete.

questions.prompt: Discuss the impact of dual-earner families on family life, with reference to role conflict and the distribution of parental and home-care responsibilities.
questions.model: Dual-earner family: both partners are in paid employment. Role conflict: the expectations of one role clash with another, for example a sick child needing a parent at home while a work deadline requires the parent to stay at work; a parent must choose a priority and may feel guilt; partners may compete over career priorities or one may not support the other's employment. Distribution of parental responsibilities: partners share supervision, transport, homework and emotional support; older children may take on extra duties; outside help such as paid childcare or relatives may take over some tasks. Distribution of home-care responsibilities: partners agree a fair division of cooking, cleaning and laundry; labour-saving appliances reduce the time needed. Positive impacts: higher household income and lower financial worry; children become more independent and learn that care is shared. Negative impacts: less time for shared family activities, weaker relationships, children feeling lonely or neglected, and childcare costs absorbing much of the second income. Reconciling strategies: flexitime, job-sharing, parental leave, career breaks and teleworking allow parents to fit work around family needs.
